title: Epidemiology and resistance patterns of urinary tract infection pathogens: A three-year study in eight hospitals in Lebanon
content:
by Shadi Eid, Mikel Karam, Omar Jamal, Rana Attieh, Serena Youssef, Yasmina Sfeir, Mona Youssef, Tarek Madani, Sola Aoun Bahous, Mariana Helou, Ibrahim Ismail, Hanane El Ahmadieh, Emma Abboud, Edmond Abboud, Zeina Shatila, Mohammad Abdallah, Kamar El Hajj Sleiman, Tamima Jisr, Fatima Jaffal, Sanaa Zoghbi, Rima Moghnieh, Rola Husni

Background

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are a prevalent disease worldwide, and increasing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) complicates empirical therapy. In Lebanon, recent multicenter data describing the distribution of urinary pathogens and their antimicrobial resistance patterns remain limited. The present study aimed to characterize uropathogens and their antimicrobial resistance patterns among inpatients and outpatient urinary cultures collected across eight hospitals in Lebanon between 2021 and 2023, and to compare resistance patterns between community-acquired and healthcare-associated UTIs.

Materials and Methods

This study is a retrospective cohort study of positive urine cultures in the laboratory records between January 2021, and December 2023, from eight hospitals in Lebanon.

Results

A total of 16,954 urine culture samples were analyzed. Gram–negative bacteria were responsible for 81% of positive urine cultures, with Escherichia coli (E. coli) (70.3%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae) (12.4%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) (4.8%), Proteus mirabilis (P. mirabilis) (4.3%), and Enterococcus faecalis (E. faecalis) (4%) being the prevalent pathogens. E. coli showed resistance to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (51%), fluoroquinolones (48%), third-generation cephalosporins (45%), and nitrofurantoin (12%). Third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolone resistance in healthcare-associated E. coli strains was significantly higher. K. pneumoniae resistance to antibiotics included nitrofurantoin (61%), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (42%), fluoroquinolones (40%), and third-generation cephalosporins (39%). Among healthcare-associated isolates E. coli (35%) was the most common, followed by Candida albicans (C. albicans) (15%), P. aeruginosa (7.6%), and K. pneumoniae (7.1%). P. aeruginosa resistance to carbapenems (40%) and fluoroquinolones (28%) is higher in healthcare-acquired setting compared to the community setting – found to be 36.08% and 37.3% respectively. This study confirms increasing antimicrobial resistance in Lebanon, consistent with trends reported in other countries.

Conclusion

This study highlights the growing challenge of AMR in UTIs, particularly in healthcare-associated infections. A comprehensive understanding of resistance patterns is critical for optimizing empirical antibiotic treatment and improving patient outcomes.
